}}'''Antonio Lanzavecchia''' (born 9 October 1951) is an Italian [[immunologist]]. He heads the Human Immunology Program at the Istituto Nazionale di Genetica Molecolare (INGM) in [[Milan]]. He worked in Switzerland for most of his career: from 1983 to 1999 at the [[Basel Institute for Immunology]], from 1999 to 2020 as founding director of the Institute for Research in Biomedicine (IRB) in [[Bellinzona]], as professor of human immunology at [[ETH Zurich]] from 2009 to 2017, where he is professor emeritus<ref name=":1">{{Cite web |title=ETH Zurich |url=https://micro.biol.ethz.ch/people/person-detail.html |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=micro.biol.ethz.ch |language=en}}</ref>, and thereafter at the Faculty of Biomedical Sciences of the [[Università della Svizzera italiana]]<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Lanzavecchia, Antonio |url=https://search.usi.ch/en/people/80896433dd0440f696fdfd2edc1b47b2/lanzavecchia-antonio |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=Università della Svizzera italiana |language=en}}</ref>. He is the scientific founder of the antibody company Humabs BioMed, acquired by [[Vir Biotechnology]] in 2017, where he was senior vice-president and senior research fellow until 2026<ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=Vir Biotechnology Appoints Leading Immunologist Antonio Lanzavecchia, M.D., Senior Vice President, Senior Research Fellow |url=https://investors.vir.bio/news/news-details/2017/Vir-Biotechnology-Appoints-Leading-Immunologist-Antonio-Lanzavecchia-M.D.-Senior-Vice-President-Senior-Research-Fellow-12-18-2017/default.aspx |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=investors.vir.bio |language=en-US}}</ref>.

Working almost exclusively with human cells, Lanzavecchia showed that B cells capture and present antigen to helper T cells, introduced the derivation of [[Dendritic cell|dendritic cells]] from blood monocytes and defined their maturation programme, proposed the serial-triggering model of [[T cell receptor]] signalling, and identified central and effector memory T cells. From 2003 his laboratory developed methods to interrogate human memory B cells and plasma cells at high throughput, yielding [[Broadly neutralizing antibody|broadly neutralising antibodies]] against influenza viruses, [[Human betaherpesvirus 5|cytomegalovirus]], coronaviruses and [[Ebola virus]], and the discovery that antibodies raised against ''[[Plasmodium falciparum]]'' can acquire whole receptor domains by templated DNA insertion.

==Education and Career==
Lanzavecchia was born in [[Varese]] and, as a fellow of the [[Collegio Borromeo]], graduated in medicine with honours from the [[University of Pavia]] in 1976, where he subsequently specialised in [[paediatrics]] and in [[infectious diseases]]. After early work at the [[University of Genoa]], he joined the [[Basel Institute for Immunology]] in 1983 and remained there until 1999.

In 1999 he founded the Institute for Research in Biomedicine in Bellinzona and directed it until 2020. He was full professor of human immunology at the Institute of Microbiology of [[ETH Zurich]] from 2009 to 2017 and remains professor emeritus there<ref name=":1" />, and was subsequently professor at the Faculty of Biomedical Sciences of the Università della Svizzera italiana<ref name=":2" />. He has also taught immunology at the University of Genoa and the [[University of Siena]]. He is now based in Italy, where he heads the Human Immunology Program at INGM in Milan. His work has been supported by three consecutive Advanced Grants of the [[European Research Council]] (IMMUNExplore, 2010–2015; BROADimmune, 2015–2020; ENGRAB, 2020–2025).

Lanzavecchia is the scientific founder of Humabs BioMed. The company began in 2004 as an incubator within the IRB, set up to develop and optimise the two antibody-isolation platforms devised in his laboratory, and was spun out as an independent company in 2011 with [[William J. Rutter]], co-founder of [[Chiron Corporation]], as founding investor and chairman of the board; Lanzavecchia served as chief scientific officer<ref>{{Cite web |title=Bellinzona spin-out: Proprietary human antibody company Humabs BioMed launches {{!}} Science{{!}}Business |url=https://sciencebusiness.net/news/75396/Bellinzona-spin-out%3A-Proprietary-human-antibody-company-Humabs-BioMed-launches |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=sciencebusiness.net |language=en}}</ref>. He is named as an inventor on the patents covering these platforms and a number of the antibodies isolated with them, which formed the basis of the company's portfolio. Humabs was acquired by Vir Biotechnology in October 2017<ref>{{Cite web |title=Humabs BioMed |url=https://www.swissbiotech.org/success-story/humabs-biomed/ |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=Swiss Biotech |language=en-US}}</ref>, and in December of that year Lanzavecchia was appointed senior vice-president and senior research fellow at Vir, a position he held until 2026<ref name=":3" />.

== Research ==
Much of Lanzavecchia's work from the early 1990s onwards was carried out jointly with the immunologist [[Federica Sallusto]]. The collaboration began at the Basel Institute for Immunology and continued after she joined him in Bellinzona following his appointment there<ref>{{Cite web |last=Switzerland |first=Albadream Engineering-Software development in Lugano |title=25 years IRB |url=https://irb.usi.ch/25-years-irb/ |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=IRB USI |language=en-US}}</ref>, and their co-authored papers span the period from 1994<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sallusto |first1=F. |last2=Lanzavecchia |first2=A. |date=1994 |title=Efficient presentation of soluble antigen by cultured human dendritic cells is maintained by granulocyte/macrophage colony-stimulating factor plus interleukin 4 and downregulated by tumor necrosis factor alpha |journal=Journal of Experimental Medicine (Journal) |volume=179 |issue=4 |pages=1109–1118 |doi=10.1084/jem.179.4.1109 |pmc=2191432 |pmid=8145033 }}</ref> to the 2020s<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Paparoditis |first=P. |date=2024 |title=Site-specific serology unveils cross-reactive monoclonal antibodies targeting influenza A hemagglutinin epitopes |journal=European Journal of Immunology |volume=54 |issue=10 |article-number=2451045 |doi=10.1002/eji.202451045 |pmid=39031535 |hdl=20.500.11850/685539 |hdl-access=free }}</ref>. They include the derivation of dendritic cells from blood monocytes, the chemokine receptor programmes of polarised T helper cells<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sallusto |first1=F. |last2=Lenig |first2=D. |last3=Mackay |first3=C.R. |last4=Lanzavecchia |first4=A. |date=1998 |title=Flexible programs of chemokine receptor expression on human polarized T helper 1 and 2 lymphocytes |journal=Journal of Experimental Medicine |volume=187 |issue=6 |pages=875–883 |doi=10.1084/jem.187.6.875 |pmid=9500790 |pmc=2212187 }}</ref>, the definition of central and effector memory T cells<ref name=":4">{{Cite journal |last=Sallusto |first=F. |date=1999 |title=Two subsets of memory T lymphocytes with distinct homing potentials and effector functions |journal=Nature |volume=401 |issue=6754 |pages=708–712 |doi=10.1038/44385 |pmid=10537110 |bibcode=1999Natur.401..708S }}</ref>, the synergistic action of Toll-like receptor agonist combinations on dendritic cells<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last=Napolitani |first=G. |date=2005 |title=Selected Toll-like receptor agonist combinations synergistically trigger a T helper type 1-polarizing program in dendritic cells |journal=[[Nature Immunology (journal)|]] |volume=6 |issue=8 |pages=769–776 |doi=10.1038/ni1223 |pmid=15995707 |pmc=3760217 |via=3760217}}</ref>, the differentiation requirements of human Th17 cells<ref name=":6">{{Cite journal |last1=Acosta-Rodriguez |first1=E.V. |last2=Napolitani |first2=G. |last3=Lanzavecchia |first3=A. |last4=Sallusto |first4=F. |date=2007 |title=Interleukins 1beta and 6 but not transforming growth factor-beta are essential for the differentiation of interleukin 17-producing human T helper cells |journal=Nature Immunology |volume=8 |issue=9 |pages=942–949 |doi=10.1038/ni1496 |pmid=17676045}}</ref>, and the analysis of the human antibody response to malaria.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Chen |first=Y. |date=2021 |title=Structural basis of malaria RIFIN binding by LILRB1-containing antibodies |journal=Nature |volume=592 |issue=7855 |pages=639–643 |doi=10.1038/s41586-021-03378-6 |pmid=33790470 |pmc=8068667 |bibcode=2021Natur.592..639C }}</ref>

== Antigen presentation and dendritic cells ==
In 1985, using antigen-specific human T and B cell clones, Lanzavecchia demonstrated that B cells use surface immunoglobulin to capture, process and present antigen to helper T cells at concentrations orders of magnitude below those required by other antigen-presenting cells.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lanzavecchia |first=A. |date=1985 |title=Antigen-specific interaction between T and B cells |journal=Nature |volume=314 |issue=6011 |pages=537–539 |doi=10.1038/314537a0 |pmid=3157869 |bibcode=1985Natur.314..537L }}</ref> The finding defined the molecular basis of T–B cooperation and provides the rationale for [[Conjugate vaccine|glycoconjugate vaccines]]. Related work established that peptides associate essentially irreversibly with MHC class II molecules in living cells,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lanzavecchia |first1=Antonio |last2=Reid |first2=P.A. |last3=Watts |first3=C. |date=1992 |title=Irreversible association of peptides with class II MHC molecules in living cells |journal=Nature |volume=357 |issue=6372 |pages=249–252 |doi=10.1038/357249a0 |pmid=1375347 |bibcode=1992Natur.357..249L }}</ref> that class II molecules present processed self proteins,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Panina-Bordignon |first=P. |date=1991 |title=Recognition by class II alloreactive T cells of processed determinants from human serum proteins |journal=Science |volume=252 |issue=5012 |pages=1548–1550 |doi=10.1126/science.1710827 |pmid=1710827 |bibcode=1991Sci...252.1548P }}</ref> and that inflammatory stimuli redistribute class II complexes to the surface of dendritic cells.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cella |first=M. |date=1997 |title=Inflammatory stimuli induce accumulation of MHC class II complexes on dendritic cells |journal=Nature |volume=388 |issue=6644 |pages=782–787 |doi=10.1038/42030 |pmid=9285591 |bibcode=1997Natur.388..782C }}</ref>

In 1994, Sallusto and Lanzavecchia showed that human blood monocytes cultured with GM-CSF and interleukin-4 differentiate into cells with the properties of immature tissue dendritic cells.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sallusto |first1=Federica |last2=Lanzavecchia |first2=Antonio |date=1994 |title=Efficient presentation of soluble antigen by cultured human dendritic cells is maintained by granulocyte/macrophage colony-stimulating factor plus interleukin 4 and downregulated by tumor necrosis factor alpha |journal=Journal of Experimental Medicine |volume=179 |issue=4 |pages=1109–1118 |doi=10.1084/jem.179.4.1109 |pmc=2191432 |pmid=8145033}}</ref> The protocol made human dendritic cells broadly accessible and became a standard reagent in the field. Using these cells the laboratory characterised antigen capture by macropinocytosis and the mannose receptor,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Sallusto |first=F. |date=1995 |title=Dendritic cells use macropinocytosis and the mannose receptor to concentrate macromolecules in the major histocompatibility complex class II compartment |journal=Journal of Experimental Medicine |volume=182 |issue=2 |pages=389–400 |doi=10.1084/jem.182.2.389 |pmc=2192110 |pmid=7629501}}</ref> and later showed that selected combinations of [[Toll-like receptor]] agonists act synergistically to drive a T helper 1-polarising programme.<ref name=":5" />

== T cell activation and immunological memory ==
In 1995 the laboratory reported that a small number of peptide–MHC complexes can serially engage and downmodulate many T cell receptors, providing a kinetic explanation for T cell sensitivity.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Valitutti |first=S. |date=1995 |title=Serial triggering of many T-cell receptors by a few peptide-MHC complexes |journal=Nature |volume=375 |issue=6527 |pages=148–151 |doi=10.1038/375148a0 |pmid=7753171 |bibcode=1995Natur.375..148V }}</ref> This was extended by the proposal that the number of receptors engaged, rather than a fixed affinity threshold, determines activation, and that costimulation lowers this tunable threshold,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Viola |first1=A. |last2=Lanzavecchia |first2=Antonio |date=1996 |title=T cell activation determined by T cell receptor number and tunable thresholds |journal=Science |volume=273 |issue=5271 |pages=104–106 |doi=10.1126/science.273.5271.104 |pmid=8658175 |bibcode=1996Sci...273..104V }}</ref> in part by reorganising membrane microdomains.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Viola |first=A. |date=1999 |title=T lymphocyte costimulation mediated by reorganization of membrane microdomains |journal=Science |volume=283 |issue=5402 |pages=680–682 |doi=10.1126/science.283.5402.680 |pmid=9924026 |bibcode=1999Sci...283..680V }}</ref> In 1999, Sallusto and Lanzavecchia divided human memory T cells into central memory and effector memory subsets, distinguished by CCR7 expression, homing behaviour and effector function.<ref name=":4" /> The distinction is now standard in the analysis of vaccine responses and of adoptive cell therapy products. Work on human T helper subsets subsequently showed that interleukin-1β and interleukin-6, rather than transforming growth factor-β as in the mouse, are required for the differentiation of interleukin-17-producing cells,<ref name=":6" /> and defined the surface phenotype and antigenic specificity of human Th17 memory cells.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Acosta-Rodriguez |first=E.V. |date=2007 |title=Surface phenotype and antigenic specificity of human interleukin 17-producing T helper memory cells |journal=Nature Immunology |volume=8 |issue=6 |pages=639–646 |doi=10.1038/ni1467 |pmid=17486092}}</ref>

== Human monoclonal antibodies and vaccine design ==
An early translational application came in 1987, when Lanzavecchia and Doris Scheidegger produced bispecific antibodies by fusing a hypoxanthine–aminopterin–thymidine-sensitive, G418-resistant anti-CD3 hybridoma with a second antibody-producing cell, so that reassortment of heavy and light chains in the resulting hybrid hybridoma yielded molecules with one arm against CD3 and one against a chosen target.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lanzavecchia |first1=A. |last2=Scheidegger |first2=D. |date=1987 |title=The use of hybrid hybridomas to target human cytotoxic T lymphocytes |journal=European Journal of Immunology |volume=17 |issue=1 |pages=105–111 |doi=10.1002/eji.1830170118 |pmid=3102250}}</ref> Such antibodies bridge human cytotoxic T lymphocytes to any cell bearing the target antigen and trigger its lysis; the strategy was demonstrated against HLA molecules, human immunoglobulins, ''[[Toxoplasma gondii]]'' and an ovarian carcinoma antigen, and is a precursor of the CD3-based [[Bispecific antibody|bispecific T cell engagers]] later developed for cancer therapy. One such reagent, OC/TR, combining anti-CD3 with the MOv18 antibody against the [[folate receptor]] of ovarian carcinoma, was characterised with the Istituto Nazionale dei Tumori in Milan<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mezzanica |first1=D. |last2=Canevari |first2=S. |last3=Ménard |first3=S. |last4=Pupa |first4=S.M. |last5=Tagliabue |first5=E. |last6=Lanzavecchia |first6=A. |last7=Colnaghi |first7=M.I. |date=1988 |title=Human ovarian carcinoma lysis by cytotoxic T cells targeted by bispecific monoclonal antibodies: analysis of the antibody components |journal=International Journal of Cancer |volume=41 |issue=4 |pages=609–615 |doi=10.1002/ijc.2910410422 |pmid=3258590 }}</ref> and became one of the first bispecific antibodies to reach clinical testing; in trials conducted by other groups, intraperitoneal treatment with autologous T lymphocytes retargeted by OC/TR produced responses in a proportion of patients with advanced ovarian carcinoma.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Canevari |first=S. |date=1995 |title=Regression of advanced ovarian carcinoma by intraperitoneal treatment with autologous T lymphocytes retargeted by a bispecific monoclonal antibody |journal=Journal of the National Cancer Institute |volume=87 |issue=19 |pages=1463–1469 |doi=10.1093/jnci/87.19.1463 |pmid=7674333}}</ref>

In 2004 the laboratory described an efficient method to immortalise human memory B cells with [[Epstein–Barr virus]], and used it to isolate potent neutralising antibodies against [[Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus|SARS coronavirus]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Traggiai |first=E. |date=2004 |title=An efficient method to make human monoclonal antibodies from memory B cells: potent neutralization of SARS coronavirus |journal=Nature Medicine |volume=10 |issue=8 |pages=871–875 |doi=10.1038/nm1080 |pmc=7095806 |pmid=15247913}}</ref> Antibodies isolated with this and related methods include FI6, which neutralises all influenza A subtypes tested;<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Corti |first=D. |date=2011 |title=A neutralizing antibody selected from plasma cells that binds to group 1 and group 2 influenza A hemagglutinins |journal=Science |volume=333 |issue=6044 |pages=850–856 |doi=10.1126/science.1205669 |pmid=21798894 |bibcode=2011Sci...333..850C }}</ref> MPE8, which cross-neutralises four paramyxoviruses;<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Corti |first=D. |date=2013 |title=Cross-neutralization of four paramyxoviruses by a human monoclonal antibody |journal=Nature |volume=501 |issue=7467 |pages=439–443 |doi=10.1038/nature12442 |pmid=23955151 |bibcode=2013Natur.501..439C }}</ref> mAb114, which protects against lethal Ebola virus infection<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Corti |first=D. |date=2016 |title=Protective monotherapy against lethal Ebola virus infection by a potently neutralizing antibody |journal=Science |volume=351 |issue=6279 |pages=1339–1342 |doi=10.1126/science.aad5224 |pmid=26917593 |bibcode=2016Sci...351.1339C }}</ref> and was approved by the [[Food and Drug Administration|FDA]] as [[ansuvimab]] in December 2020;<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ebanga (ansuvimab-zykl) FDA Approval History |url=https://www.drugs.com/history/ebanga.html |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=Drugs.com |language=en}}</ref> and S309, isolated from a survivor of the 2003 SARS outbreak, which cross-neutralises [[SARS-CoV-2]]<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pinto |first=D. |date=2020 |title=Cross-neutralization of SARS-CoV-2 by a human monoclonal SARS-CoV antibody |journal=Nature |volume=583 |issue=7815 |pages=290–295 |doi=10.1038/s41586-020-2349-y |pmid=32422645 |bibcode=2020Natur.583..290P }}</ref> and was developed into [[sotrovimab]], authorised for emergency use in COVID-19 in May 2021.<ref>{{Cite web |title=FDA updates sotrovimab emergency use authorization {{!}}publisher=US Food and Drug Administration |work=U.S. Food and Drug Administration |date=23 December 2024 |url=https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-safety-and-availability/fda-updates-sotrovimab-emergency-use-authorization}}</ref>

These antibodies were also used as analytical reagents to identify the epitopes that confer protection and to guide the design of the corresponding immunogen, an approach the laboratory termed analytic vaccinology. Its clearest application was to cytomegalovirus: neutralising antibodies isolated from immune donors showed that the dominant protective response is directed against the gH/gL/pUL128L pentameric complex rather than glycoprotein B, and a recombinant pentamer designed on that basis selectively elicited potent neutralising antibodies.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kabanova |first=A. |date=2014 |title=Antibody-driven design of a human cytomegalovirus gHgLpUL128L subunit vaccine that selectively elicits potent neutralizing antibodies |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=111 |issue=50 |pages=17965–17970 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1415310111 |doi-access=free |pmc=4273412 |pmid=25453106 |bibcode=2014PNAS..11117965K }}</ref> Related studies examined the mutational paths leading to antibody breadth<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pappas |first=L. |date=2014 |title=Rapid development of broadly influenza neutralizing antibodies through redundant mutations |journal=Nature |volume=516 |issue=7531 |pages=418–422 |doi=10.1038/nature13764 |pmid=25296253 |bibcode=2014Natur.516..418P }}</ref> and the somatic origin of autoantibodies in [[pemphigus]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Di Zenzo |first=G. |date=2012 |title=Pemphigus autoantibodies generated through somatic mutations target the desmoglein-3 cis-interface |journal=Journal of Clinical Investigation |volume=122 |issue=10 |pages=3781–3790 |doi=10.1172/JCI64413 |pmc=3461925 |pmid=22996451}}</ref>

== Malaria ==
From memory B cells of donors immunised with attenuated ''[[Plasmodium falciparum]]'' sporozoites the laboratory isolated a public antibody lineage, typified by MGG4, that binds both the central repeat of the [[circumsporozoite protein]] and a junctional peptide at its N terminus which is not present in the RTS,S vaccine; this dual binding was associated with potent inhibition of infection in humanised mice.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tan |first=J |date=2018 |title=A public antibody lineage that potently inhibits malaria infection through dual binding to the circumsporozoite protein |journal=Nature Medicine |volume=24 |issue=4 |pages=401–407 |doi=10.1038/nm.4513 |pmc=5893353 |pmid=29554084}}</ref> The junctional region has since become a target for antimalarial monoclonal antibodies and for immunogen design.

Screening of donors from Kenya and Mali revealed antibodies carrying large insertions of genomic DNA encoding human inhibitory receptors. In the first such antibodies the insert encodes the collagen-binding domain of [[LAIR1]] and confers broad reactivity against RIFIN variant surface antigens expressed on infected erythrocytes;<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tan |first=J. |date=2016 |title=A LAIR1 insertion generates broadly reactive antibodies against malaria variant antigens |journal=Nature |volume=529 |issue=7584 |pages=105–109 |doi=10.1038/nature16450 |pmc=4869849 |pmid=26700814 |bibcode=2016Natur.529..105T }}</ref> two distinct insertion modalities generating these public antibodies were subsequently defined.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pieper |first=K. |date=2017 |title=Public antibodies to malaria antigens generated by two LAIR1 insertion modalities |journal=Nature |volume=548 |issue=7669 |pages=597–601 |doi=10.1038/nature23670 |pmc=5635981 |pmid=28847005 |bibcode=2017Natur.548..597P }}</ref> A second class incorporates extracellular domains of the receptor LILRB1 at the variable–constant elbow and recognises a different set of RIFINs.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Chen |first=Y. |date=2021 |title=Structural basis of malaria RIFIN binding by LILRB1-containing antibodies |journal=Nature |volume=592 |issue=7855 |pages=639–643 |doi=10.1038/s41586-021-03378-6 |pmid=33790470 |pmc=8068667 |bibcode=2021Natur.592..639C }}</ref> Together the studies established templated insertion of host receptor sequences as a mechanism of antibody diversification distinct from V(D)J recombination and somatic hypermutation, and indicated that the parasite engages several inhibitory receptors as part of its immune evasion strategy.

== Honors ==
* He was elected to the [[European Molecular Biology Organization]] and, in 2016, as an international member of the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|US National Academy of Sciences]]<ref>{{Cite web |title=Antonio Lanzavecchia – NAS |url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/antonio-lanzavecchia-ktdmoc/ |access-date=2026-09-21 |website=www.nasonline.org |language=en-US}}</ref>, and is an honorary member of the Swiss Academy of Medical Sciences, the [[American Association of Immunologists]] and the Swiss Society for Allergology and Immunology. He served on the board of reviewing editors of ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' from 1997 to 2005 and as an advisory editor of the ''[[Journal of Experimental Medicine]]''.
* Three of his papers have been selected for the Pillars of Immunology series of the ''[[Journal of Immunology]]'', which reprints reports judged to have shaped the course of the field, each with a commissioned commentary: the 1985 demonstration of antigen-specific T–B cooperation,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Lanzavecchia |first=A. |date=2007 |title=Pillars Article: Antigen-specific interaction between T and B cells. Nature 1985. 314: 537-539 |journal=[[Journal of Immunology (journal)|]] |volume=179 |issue=11 |pages=7206–7208}}</ref> the 1994 derivation of dendritic cells from blood monocytes,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sallusto |first1=F. |last2=Lanzavecchia |first2=A. |date=2018 |title=Pillars Article: Efficient presentation of soluble antigen by cultured human dendritic cells is maintained by granulocyte/macrophage colony-stimulating factor plus interleukin 4 and downregulated by tumor necrosis factor alpha. J. Exp. Med. 1994. 179: 1109-1118 |journal=Journal of Immunology |volume=200 |issue=3 |pages=887–896 |pmid=29358412}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Amigorena |first=S. |date=2018 |title=Dendritic cells on the way to glory |journal=Journal of Immunology |volume=200 |issue=3 |pages=885–886 |doi=10.4049/jimmunol.1701693 |pmid=29358411}}</ref> and the 1999 division of memory T cells into central and effector subsets.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sallusto |first1=F. |last2=Lenig |first2=D. |last3=Forster |first3=R. |last4=Lipp |first4=M. |last5=Lanzavecchia |first5=A. |date=2014 |title=Pillars Article: Two subsets of memory T lymphocytes with distinct homing potentials and effector functions. ==Editorial activities==
